data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which is NOT one of the six articles of faith in Sunni Islam?
data.targetWord: Belief in justice

examples.en-GB: Answer: Belief in justice | Distractors: Belief in angels; Belief in predestination; Belief in prophets

data.sourceWord: Qur'an — direct word of Allah revealed to Muhammad
data.targetWord: The Qur'an is the direct word of Allah, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Jibril, beginning on the Night of Power (Laylatul Qadr). It is eternal and protected by Allah himself.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — beliefs about the Qur'an

data.sourceWord: Qur'an — source of guidance and worship
data.targetWord: The Qur'an is a source of guidance for all aspects of Muslim life, containing 114 surahs in Arabic. It is treated with great respect — wudu must be performed before touching it; it is memorised and recited.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — beliefs about the Qur'an

data.sourceWord: Imamate influence — infallible authority for Shi'a
data.targetWord: Shi'a Muslims follow the imams as infallible, divinely appointed successors of the Prophet. The twelve imams (Twelvers) are part of the Ahle-Bayt and their teachings guide all aspects of Muslim life.

data.sourceWord: Imamate influence — awaiting the hidden Imam
data.targetWord: Some Shi'a Muslims believe the last imam (Muhammad Mahdi) is in occultation and will return at the end of times. This influences them to live righteously and await his return.

data.sourceWord: Angel Jibril — conveyed revelation to all prophets
data.targetWord: Jibril (Gabriel) is the archangel who brought messages from Allah to all the prophets, including revealing the Qur'an to Muhammad in the cave of Hira on the Night of Power.

data.sourceWord: Angel Jibril — accompanied and assisted the Prophet
data.targetWord: Jibril cleansed the Prophet's heart in childhood, accompanied him on the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj), and assisted him throughout his life. He has wings that stretch across the seven heavens.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: Jibril in the Qur'an
data.targetWord: 'Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel — it is he who has brought the Qur'an down upon your heart by permission of Allah, confirming that which was before it and as guidance and good tidings.' (2:97)

data.sourceWord: FOR: The Qur'an continuously names Allah as merciful
data.targetWord: The Qur'an refers to God's mercy more than any other attribute; the majority of surahs begin with Bismillah, containing Ar-Rahman (Most Gracious) and Ar-Raheem (Most Merciful). Mercy begins the 99 names.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Without God's mercy none could enter heaven
data.targetWord: Muslims believe that without God's mercy they could not enter Jannah (heaven), their ultimate goal. God's mercy is what makes salvation possible; it is therefore the most essential quality of Allah.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Allah has 99 names — no single quality is supreme
data.targetWord: 'And to Allah belongs the best names, so invoke him by them.' (7:180) — each name reveals a different aspect of God's nature; mercy is one quality among many, and none alone gives a full picture.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Tawhid — oneness — is the cornerstone of Muslim belief
data.targetWord: Allah is described as One (tawhid) — this is considered the cornerstone of all Muslim belief. The Shahadah affirms his oneness first; tawhid may therefore be the most fundamental description of God.

data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which pillar of Islam involves pilgrimage to Makkah?
data.targetWord: Hajj

examples.en-GB: Answer: Hajj | Distractors: Sawm; Zakah; Salah

data.sourceWord: Salah — five daily prayers
data.targetWord: Salah (five daily prayers) is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Muslims pray at set times facing the Kaaba in Makkah, performing set positions (rakat) and reciting verses from the Qur'an.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — Islamic practices of worship

data.sourceWord: Zakah — obligatory charity
data.targetWord: Zakah (obligatory charity) is the third pillar of Islam. Muslims give 2.5% of surplus wealth annually to those in need, purifying their wealth and fulfilling their duty of care to the community.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — Islamic practices of worship

data.sourceWord: Sawm — fasting in Ramadan as spiritual discipline
data.targetWord: During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, refraining from food, drink and sexual relations. Fasting builds taqwa (God-consciousness), self-discipline, and empathy for the poor.

data.sourceWord: Sawm — community unity and revelation
data.targetWord: Ramadan commemorates the first revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad. The communal iftar (breaking of the fast) strengthens community bonds; it concludes with the celebration of Eid ul-Fitr.

data.sourceWord: Hajj — unity of the Ummah
data.targetWord: Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah) is the fifth pillar, required once in a lifetime for those able. All pilgrims wear ihram (simple white garments), symbolising equality before Allah regardless of wealth or status.

data.sourceWord: Hajj — following Ibrahim's example
data.targetWord: The rituals of Hajj commemorate the trials of Ibrahim, Hajar and Ismail. Circling the Kaaba (tawaf), walking between Safa and Marwa, and standing on the plain of Arafat all re-enact their submission to Allah.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: the obligation of Hajj
data.targetWord: 'And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people who are able to undertake it.' (3:97) — establishing Hajj as a divine command for all capable Muslims.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Salah is most important — performed five times daily
data.targetWord: Salah is performed five times every day, making it the most regular and constant act of worship in a Muslim's life. It structures each day around submission to Allah and is the second pillar of Islam.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Shahadah is more fundamental — it makes one Muslim
data.targetWord: The Shahadah (declaration of faith) is the first pillar and the gateway to all other acts of worship. Without it a person is not Muslim, making it logically more fundamental than Salah.

data.prompt: What are the Five Pillars of Islam?
data.answer: The Five Pillars are Shahadah Salah Zakah Sawm and Hajj.

data.prompt: What does Zakah require Muslims to give?
data.answer: Zakah requires Muslims to give two point five percent of their wealth.
Hajj commemorates the trials of Ibrahim and his family.

data.title: The Five Pillars of Islam
data.sourcePassage: The Five Pillars are the core practices that every Muslim is expected to follow. Together they form the framework of Muslim life and worship. The Shahadah (declaration of faith) states: 'There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is his messenger.' It is the entry point to Islam and is whispered into a newborn's ear. Salah (prayer) is performed five times daily — at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, and night — always facing the Kaaba in Makkah. Zakah (charitable giving) requires Muslims to give 2.5% of their surplus wealth to the poor and needy each year, purifying the giver and redistributing wealth. Sawm (fasting) during Ramadan involves abstaining from food, drink and sexual relations from dawn to sunset, building self-discipline and remembrance of those who go hungry. Hajj (pilgrimage) to Makkah must be completed at least once in a lifetime by every Muslim who is physically and financially able. It unites Muslims from every nation in acts of worship that trace back to the Prophet Ibrahim.
